expectedText:
INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY LICENSE BANKRUPTCY PROTECTIONS (11 U.S.C. § 365(N)) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY LICENSE BANKRUPTCY PROTECTIONS INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes what happens, as a matter of federal Bankruptcy Code law, to a license of intellectual property when the licensor -- not the licensee -- becomes a debtor in a federal bankruptcy case and rejects the license as part of that case. It is prepared by Jordan T. Reyes on behalf of Acme, Inc., as licensee, concerning intellectual property licensed from Beta Corp. and described as follows: U.S. Patent No. 10,123,456, licensed under the parties' March 2023 patent license agreement. This Information Sheet is a general informational reference describing the general bankruptcy rule that a debtor's rejection of an executory contract operates as a breach rather than a rescission, the specific statutory protections 11 U.S.C. section 365(n) gives a licensee of certain kinds of intellectual property when its licensor's contract is rejected, which categories of intellectual property that statute's own definition does and does not reach, and how the U.S. Supreme Court has since resolved what happens to a category the statute's definition does not reach (trademark licenses). It does not itself determine what protection would apply to the intellectual property described above in any actual bankruptcy case, and it is not a substitute for that case-specific legal determination. This document is distinct from this project's existing Software License Agreement, Patent License Agreement, and Trademark License Agreement documents, none of which addresses what becomes of a licensee's rights if the licensor later files for bankruptcy protection; it is also distinct from the existing Trade Secret Preemption Doctrine and Trade Secret Injunctive Relief Standards Information Sheets, which concern trade secret litigation remedies rather than a licensor's bankruptcy.

THE GENERAL RULE: REJECTION OF AN EXECUTORY CONTRACT IS A BREACH, NOT A RESCISSION
When a business licensor files for bankruptcy, the trustee or debtor-in-possession has authority under 11 U.S.C. section 365(a) to decide whether to assume or reject the licensor's executory contracts, which can include an intellectual property license under which royalties or performance are still owed on both sides. Section 365(g) states the legal effect of that choice when the trustee rejects: rejection of an executory contract is treated as if the debtor had simply broken the contract, not as if the contract had been undone from the start. The U.S. Supreme Court has confirmed what this means in practice: because rejection is a breach and not a rescission, it does not by itself take back the rights the contract had already conveyed to the counterparty before the bankruptcy case began -- the same result that would follow if the licensor breached the same contract outside of bankruptcy.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "the rejection of an executory contract or unexpired lease of the debtor constitutes a breach of such contract or lease"
  — 11 U.S.C. § 365(g) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Bankruptcy Code, effect of rejection of an executory contract (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/11/365)
  "We hold it does not. A rejection breaches a contract but does not rescind it."
  — Mission Product Holdings, Inc. v. Tempnology, LLC, No. 17-1657, U.S. Supreme Court, argued February 20, 2019, decided May 20, 2019 (Cornell LII slip opinion text; commonly reported as 587 U.S. 370 (2019), not independently confirmed against the bound U.S. Reports this session) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/17-1657)
  Known gap: This is federal statutory and U.S. Supreme Court law of general application, used as real evidence of the rejection-as-breach rule -- not a claim about whether any specific license described on this sheet would in fact be rejected, assumed, or treated as executory in an actual bankruptcy case, which depends on case-specific facts and the bankruptcy court's own determination that this clause does not evaluate. This is federal bankruptcy law that applies uniformly in every U.S. district, including the U.S. Bankruptcy Courts for California's four federal districts; it is not a California-specific rule, though it routinely governs California businesses' IP licenses.

WHAT COUNTS AS "INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY" FOR THIS STATUTE'S PROTECTION
The special licensee protection in 11 U.S.C. section 365(n), described in the following clauses, applies only to a defined list of property. The Bankruptcy Code's own definitions section, 11 U.S.C. section 101(35A), defines "intellectual property" for this purpose as a closed list of six categories: a trade secret; an invention, process, design, or plant protected under patent law (title 35); a patent application; a plant variety; a work of authorship protected under copyright law (title 17); or a semiconductor mask work protected under chapter 9 of title 17 -- each only to the extent it is actually protected under the applicable non-bankruptcy law that governs it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "means— (A) trade secret; (B) invention, process, design, or plant protected under title 35; (C) patent application; (D) plant variety; (E) work of authorship protected under title 17; or (F) mask work protected under chapter 9 of title 17; to the extent protected by applicable nonbankruptcy law."
  — 11 U.S.C. § 101(35A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Bankruptcy Code, definition of "intellectual property" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/11/101)
  Known gap: This is federal statutory law, used as real evidence of the closed six-category list in 11 U.S.C. section 101(35A) -- not a claim about whether the specific intellectual property described on this sheet falls within any of these six categories or is in fact protected under the applicable non-bankruptcy law that would have to protect it (patent, copyright, trade secret, or plant variety law), which this clause does not evaluate. This definition is federal and uniform nationwide; it is not a California-specific statute, though California-based licensees and licensors routinely rely on it.

TRADEMARKS ARE NOT WITHIN THIS STATUTE'S DEFINITION
The six-category definition described in the preceding clause does not list a trademark, trade name, or service mark among the property it covers. The U.S. Supreme Court has confirmed the consequence of that omission directly: the licensee protection statute, 11 U.S.C. section 365(n), does not cover trademark licensing agreements at all. Because that specific statute does not reach trademark licenses, a rejected trademark license instead falls back on the general rejection-as-breach rule described in the first clause of this Information Sheet, rather than on the specific retained-rights mechanics section 365(n) provides for the six listed categories, which are described in the clauses that follow.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "that provision does not cover trademark licensing agreements, which continue to fall, along with most other contracts, within Section 365(g)’s general rule."
  — Mission Product Holdings, Inc. v. Tempnology, LLC, No. 17-1657, U.S. Supreme Court, argued February 20, 2019, decided May 20, 2019 (Cornell LII slip opinion text; commonly reported as 587 U.S. 370 (2019), not independently confirmed against the bound U.S. Reports this session) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/17-1657)
  Known gap: This is federal statutory law and a real, verified U.S. Supreme Court statement about that statute's scope, used as real evidence that trademarks fall outside 11 U.S.C. section 365(n)'s definition -- not a claim about how any specific trademark license would be treated in an actual bankruptcy case. The Bankruptcy Code's text itself does not contain an express sentence stating that trademarks are excluded; this clause's second citation is to the Supreme Court's own description of that consequence of the statute's closed list, which this clause treats as the operative statement of the exclusion rather than independently construing the omission itself. This is federal law of general application, not California-specific.

THE LICENSEE'S CHOICE WHEN A COVERED LICENSE IS REJECTED
For a license within the six covered categories, section 365(n) gives the licensee -- not the trustee -- the choice of how to respond to the licensor's rejection. The licensee may elect to treat the contract as terminated by the rejection, to the same extent it could have treated the contract as terminated by a breach outside of bankruptcy, and pursue a damage claim for that breach. Alternatively, the licensee may instead elect to retain its rights under the license and any supplementary agreement to the licensed intellectual property, as those rights existed immediately before the bankruptcy case began, for the remaining duration of the contract and any extension period the licensee is entitled to exercise as of right. That retained-rights election includes the right to enforce any exclusivity provision the license contains, but the statute expressly withholds one specific remedy from it: any other right the licensee might otherwise have, under applicable non-bankruptcy law, to force specific performance of the contract.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "to retain its rights (including a right to enforce any exclusivity provision of such contract, but excluding any other right under applicable nonbankruptcy law to specific performance of such contract) under such contract and under any agreement supplementary to such contract, to such intellectual property (including any embodiment of such intellectual property to the extent protected by applicable nonbankruptcy law), as such rights existed immediately before the case commenced"
  — 11 U.S.C. § 365(n)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Bankruptcy Code, licensee's election on licensor's rejection of an intellectual property license (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/11/365)
  Known gap: This is federal statutory law, used as real evidence of the two-option election 11 U.S.C. section 365(n)(1) gives a licensee of covered intellectual property -- not a claim about which option would be more advantageous for any specific licensee described on this sheet, or that either election has actually been made in any pending or contemplated bankruptcy case, which are case-specific business and legal decisions this clause does not evaluate. This is federal law of general application, not California-specific.

WHAT THE TRUSTEE MUST DO -- AND WHAT THE LICENSEE MUST KEEP PAYING -- IF RIGHTS ARE RETAINED
If the licensee elects to retain its rights rather than treat the license as terminated, section 365(n)(2) imposes matching obligations on both sides of the relationship. The trustee is required to let the licensee actually exercise the rights it elected to retain. On the licensee's side, retaining rights is not free: the licensee must keep making all royalty payments due under the contract for its remaining duration and for any extension period the licensee exercises, and in exchange for retaining its rights the licensee is deemed to waive any right of setoff it might otherwise have against the estate under the Bankruptcy Code or applicable non-bankruptcy law, as well as any administrative-expense claim under section 503(b) arising from the contract's performance. On written request, the trustee must also turn over any of the licensed intellectual property (or protected embodiments of it) that the trustee is holding, to the extent the contract provides for that, and must not interfere with the licensee's contractual rights to that intellectual property, including the licensee's right to obtain it from someone other than the trustee.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "the trustee shall allow the licensee to exercise such rights"
  — 11 U.S.C. § 365(n)(2)(A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Bankruptcy Code, trustee's obligation to allow the licensee to exercise retained rights (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/11/365)
  "the licensee shall make all royalty payments due under such contract for the duration of such contract and for any period described in paragraph (1)(B) of this subsection for which the licensee extends such contract"
  — 11 U.S.C. § 365(n)(2)(B) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Bankruptcy Code, licensee's continuing royalty obligation on retaining rights (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/11/365)
  Known gap: This is federal statutory law, used as real evidence of the trustee's and the retaining licensee's respective statutory obligations under 11 U.S.C. section 365(n)(2) and (3) -- not a claim that any specific trustee, debtor, or licensee described on this sheet has performed or failed to perform these obligations in an actual case, which this clause does not evaluate. The royalty-payment quotation is drawn from paragraph (n)(2); the trustee's turn-over and non-interference obligations described in the final two sentences of this clause's body come from the separate written-request mechanism in paragraph (n)(3), which is not independently quoted here beyond the one royalty-payment sentence cited below. This is federal law of general application, not California-specific.

THE SUPREME COURT'S RESOLUTION FOR CATEGORIES THE STATUTE DOES NOT COVER
Before 2019, federal appellate courts disagreed about what happened to a licensee's rights when a licensor rejected a license that section 365(n) did not cover, such as a trademark license -- some courts reasoned that Congress's decision to spell out retained-rights protection for the six listed categories meant Congress intended rejection to extinguish a licensee's rights in every other kind of contract. The U.S. Supreme Court rejected that reasoning in Mission Product Holdings, Inc. v. Tempnology, LLC, holding that rejection of a contract of any kind in bankruptcy operates as a breach and not as a rescission, so that a trademark licensee's rights survive rejection in the same way any other counterparty's contractual rights survive a rejection, even though no statute spells that out specifically for trademarks the way section 365(n) does for the six listed categories.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]

  — Mission Product Holdings, Inc. v. Tempnology, LLC, No. 17-1657, U.S. Supreme Court, argued February 20, 2019, decided May 20, 2019 (Cornell LII slip opinion text; commonly reported as 587 U.S. 370 (2019), not independently confirmed against the bound U.S. Reports this session) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/17-1657)

WHY SECTION 365(N) EXISTS: THE 1988 RESPONSE TO A FOURTH CIRCUIT PATENT-LICENSE RULING
Section 365(n) was not part of the Bankruptcy Code as originally enacted; Congress added it in 1988 in direct response to a specific federal appellate decision. In Lubrizol Enterprises v. Richmond Metal Finishers, the Fourth Circuit had held that a debtor-licensor's rejection of an executory patent license contract worked to revoke the license it had granted, stripping the licensee of its right to keep using the patented technology. Congress responded by enacting section 365(n) specifically to reverse that ruling and ensure that licensees of patents (and the other categories later listed in the statute) keep the rights described in the preceding clauses even when their licensor's contract is rejected in bankruptcy.

Tempnology, LLC, not from an independent fetch of the Fourth Circuit's 1985 Lubrizol opinion itself (756 F.2d 1043), which this session did not separately retrieve from a primary source -- this session's CourtListener access was rate-limited (125 requests/day, exhausted) when this clause's research was performed. The date this clause treats as when section 365(n) was enacted (1988) and its statutory citation come from the Supreme Court's own opinion text, which cites Pub. L. 100-506, 102 Stat. 2538 (1988), for that enactment; this clause does not independently verify the Statutes at Large volume and page against a primary Statutes at Large source. This is federal legislative and case-law history, not California-specific.
